claim: ATAC-Seq is a widely used technique to explore gene regulatory mechanisms.
source: Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin sequencing (ATAC-Seq) is a widely used technique to explore gene regulatory mechanisms.

claim: For most ATAC-Seq data from healthy and diseased tissues such as tumors, chromatin accessibility measurement represents a mixed signal from multiple cell types.
source: For most ATAC-Seq data from healthy and diseased tissues such as tumors, chromatin accessibility measurement represents a mixed signal from multiple cell types.

claim: The authors derived reliable chromatin accessibility marker peaks and reference profiles for most non-malignant cell types frequently observed in the microenvironment of human tumors.

evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data and analyses presented. The citation to Racle et al., 2017 provides additional support.

claim: The EPIC-ATAC tool accurately predicts non-malignant and malignant cell fractions in tumor samples.
source: Our EPIC-ATAC tool accurately predicts non-malignant and malignant cell fractions in tumor samples.

claim: When applied to a human breast cancer cohort, EPIC-ATAC accurately infers the immune contexture of the main breast cancer subtypes.
source: When applied to a human breast cancer cohort, EPIC-ATAC accurately infers the immune contexture of the main breast cancer subtypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of the breast cancer cohort presented in the results section.

claim: The genome-wide landscape of chromatin accessibility varies in different cell types.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Klemm et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021b).

claim: Over the last decade, ATAC-Seq has become a reference epigenomic technique to profile chromatin accessibility and the activity of gene regulatory elements in diverse biological contexts including cancer.
source: Over the last decade, Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin (ATAC-Seq; Buenrostro et al., 2013) has become a reference epigenomic technique to profile chromatin accessibility and the activity of gene regulatory elements in diverse biological contexts including cancer (Luo et al., 2022) and across large cohorts (Corces et al., 2018).

claim: ATAC-Seq has been used to profile chromatin accessibility across large cohorts.
source: Over the last decade, Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin (ATAC-Seq; Buenrostro et al., 2013) has become a reference epigenomic technique to profile chromatin accessibility and the activity of gene regulatory elements in diverse biological contexts including cancer (Luo et al., 2022) and across large cohorts (Corces et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Corces et al., 2018).

source: Several optimized ATAC-Seq protocols have been developed to improve the quality of ATAC-Seq data and expand its usage to different tissue types.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent description of specific protocols and citations.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Corces et al., 2017; Grandi et al., 2022).

source: These include the OMNI-ATAC protocol, which leads to a cleaner signal and is applicable to frozen samples (Corces et al., 2017; Grandi et al., 2022), as well as the formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE)-ATAC protocol adapted to FFPE samples (Zhang et al., 2022b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Zhang et al., 2022b).

source: The reasonable cost and technical advantages of these protocols foreshadow an increased usage of ATAC-Seq in cancer studies (Grandi et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future trends, supported by citations to prior research (Grandi et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2022).

claim: Most biological tissues are composed of multiple cell types.
source: Most biological tissues are composed of multiple cell types.

source: For instance, tumors are complex ecosystems including malignant and stromal cells as well as a large diversity of immune cells.

source: Most existing ATAC-Seq data from tumors were performed on bulk samples, thereby mixing the signal from both cancer and non-malignant cells.

source: Precisely quantifying the proportions of different cell types in such samples represents a promising way to explore the immune contexture and the composition of the tumor microenvironment (TME) across large cohorts.

claim: Carefully assessing cell-type heterogeneity is important in handling confounding factors in genomic analyses in which samples with different cellular compositions are compared.
source: Carefully assessing cell-type heterogeneity is also important in handling confounding factors in genomic analyses in which samples with different cellular compositions are compared.

claim: Single-cell ATAC-Seq has been developed to explore cellular heterogeneity with high resolution in complex biological systems.
source: Recently, single-cell ATAC-Seq (scATAC-Seq) has been developed to explore cellular heterogeneity with high resolution in complex biological systems (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Lareau et al., 2019; Satpathy et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Cusanovich et al., 2015; Lareau et al., 2019; Satpathy et al., 2019).

claim: Single-cell ATAC-Seq data are sensitive to technical noise.
source: However, the resulting data are sensitive to technical noise and such experiments require important resources, which so far limits the use of scATAC-Seq in contrast to bulk ATAC-Seq in the context of large cohorts.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the limitations of single-cell ATAC-Seq technology.

claim: Single-cell ATAC-Seq experiments require important resources, which limits the use of scATAC-Seq in contrast to bulk ATAC-Seq in the context of large cohorts.

claim: In the past decade, computational deconvolution tools have been developed to predict the proportion of diverse cell types from bulk genomic data obtained from tumor samples.
source: In the past decade, computational deconvolution tools have been developed to predict the proportion of diverse cell types from bulk genomic data obtained from tumor samples (Becht et al., 2016; Racle et al., 2017; Avila Cobos et al., 2018; Avila Cobos et al., 2020; Finotello et al., 2019; Monaco et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2019; Sturm et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Becht et al., 2016; Racle et al., 2017; Avila Cobos et al., 2018; Avila Cobos et al., 2020; Finotello et al., 2019; Monaco et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2019; Sturm et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020b).

claim: Many deconvolution tools model bulk data as a mixture of reference profiles either coming from purified cell populations or inferred from single-cell genomic data for each cell type.
source: As described in more detail elsewhere (Avila Cobos et al., 2018; Sturm et al., 2019), many of these tools model bulk data as a mixture of reference profiles either coming from purified cell populations or inferred from single-cell genomic data for each cell type.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Avila Cobos et al., 2018; Sturm et al., 2019).

claim: The accuracy of cell-type proportion predictions relies on the quality of reference profiles as well as on the specificity of cell-type markers.
source: The accuracy of cell-type proportion predictions relies on the quality of these reference profiles as well as on the specificity of cell-type markers (Avila Cobos et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Avila Cobos et al., 2018).

claim: A limitation of most deconvolution algorithms is that they do not predict the proportion of cell types that are not present in the reference profiles.
source: A limitation of most deconvolution algorithms is that they do not predict the proportion of cell types that are not present in the reference profiles (hereafter referred to as 'uncharacterized' cells).
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the limitations of existing deconvolution algorithms.

claim: In the context of tumor samples, uncharacterized cell populations include malignant cells whose molecular profiles differ not only from one cancer type to another but also from one patient to another even within the same tumor type.
source: In the context of tumor samples, these uncharacterized cell populations include malignant cells whose molecular profiles differ not only from one cancer type to another but also from one patient to another even within the same tumor type (Corces et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Corces et al., 2018).

claim: A few tools developed for bulk RNA-Seq data consider uncharacterized cells in their deconvolution framework by using cell-type specific markers not expressed in the uncharacterized cells.
source: To address this limitation, a few tools developed for bulk RNA-Seq data consider uncharacterized cells in their deconvolution framework by using cell-type specific markers not expressed in the uncharacterized cells (Gosink et al., 2007; Clarke et al., 2010; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Gosink et al., 2007; Clarke et al., 2010; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019).

claim: EPIC simultaneously quantifies immune, stromal, vascular as well as uncharacterized cells from bulk tumor samples.
source: These tools include EPIC (estimating the proportion of immune and cancer cells) which simultaneously quantifies immune, stromal, vascular as well as uncharacterized cells from bulk tumor samples (Racle et al., 2017; Racle and Gfeller, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Racle et al., 2017; Racle and Gfeller, 2020).

claim: Most deconvolution algorithms have been developed for transcriptomic data (RNA-Seq data).
source: Most deconvolution algorithms have been developed for transcriptomic data (RNA-Seq data) (Gong and Szustakowski, 2013; Newman et al., 2015; Newman et al., 2019; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019; Jiménez-Sánchez et al., 2019; Monaco et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Gong and Szustakowski, 2013; Newman et al., 2015; Newman et al., 2019; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019; Jiménez-Sánchez et al., 2019; Monaco et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020a).

claim: Deconvolution algorithms have been proposed for proteomics data.
source: More recently they have been proposed for other omics layers such as methylation (Aryee et al., 2014; Teschendorff et al., 2017; Teschendorff et al., 2020; Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Hicks and Irizarry, 2019; Rahmani et al., 2019; Arneson et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a; Salas et al., 2022), proteomics (Feng et al., 2023), or chromatin accessibility (Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Feng et al., 2023).

source: More recently they have been proposed for other omics layers such as methylation (Aryee et al., 2014; Teschendorff et al., 2017; Teschendorff et al., 2020; Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Hicks and Irizarry, 2019; Rahmani et al., 2019; Arneson et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a; Salas et al., 2022), proteomics (Feng et al., 2023), or chromatin accessibility (Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Li et al., 2020b).

source: For the latter, a specific framework called DeconPeaker (Li et al., 2020b) was developed to estimate cell-type proportions from bulk ATAC-Seq samples.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Li et al., 2020b).

source: Deconvolution tools developed initially for RNA-Seq data can also be applied to ATAC-Seq.

source: For example, the popular deconvolution tool, CIBERSORT (Newman et al., 2015), in combination with ATAC-Seq profiles, was used to deconvolve leukemic ATAC-Seq samples (Corces et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Newman et al., 2015; Corces et al., 2016).

source: The application of existing bulk ATAC-Seq data deconvolution tools to solid tumors faces some limitations.
evidence: This statement is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field, which is then elaborated upon.

source: First, current computational frameworks do not quantify populations of uncharacterized cell types.
evidence: This statement is based on the authors' knowledge of existing deconvolution frameworks for ATAC-Seq data.

source: Second, ATAC-Seq-based markers (i.e. chromatin-accessible regions called peaks) and reference profiles generated so far have been derived in the context of hematopoietic cell mixtures (Corces et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Corces et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020b).

source: Markers and profiles for major populations of the TME (e.g. stromal and vascular cells) are thus missing.

source: While cell-type specific markers have been identified from scATAC-Seq data (Zhang et al., 2021b), not all TME-relevant cell types are covered (e.g. lack of scATAC-Seq data from neutrophils due to extracellular traps formation).
evidence: This statement is supported by the example of neutrophils and the citation to prior research (Zhang et al., 2021b).

claim: There is a lack of scATAC-Seq data from neutrophils due to extracellular traps formation.
source: While cell-type specific markers have been identified from scATAC-Seq data (Zhang et al., 2021b), not all TME-relevant cell types are covered (e.g. lack of scATAC-Seq data from neutrophils due to extracellular traps formation).
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the technical challenges of performing scATAC-Seq on neutrophils.

claim: Many cell-type specific markers from scATAC-Seq data have not been curated to fulfill the requirements of tools such as EPIC to quantify uncharacterized cells.
source: Many of these markers have also not been curated to fulfill the requirements of tools such as EPIC to quantify uncharacterized cells (i.e. markers of a cell type should not be accessible in other human tissues).
evidence: This statement is based on the authors' assessment of existing markers and the requirements of the EPIC framework.

source: In this study, we collected ATAC-Seq data from pure cell types to identify cell-type specific marker peaks and to build reference profiles from most major non-malignant cell types typically observed in tumors.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented.

source: These data were integrated into the EPIC (Racle et al., 2017) framework to perform bulk ATAC-Seq samples deconvolution (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data and Figure 1.

source: Applied on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and tumor samples, the EPIC-ATAC framework showed accurate predictions of the proportions of non-malignant and malignant cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the benchmarking data presented in the results section.

claim: 564 pure ATAC-Seq data of sorted cells were collected to build reference profiles for non-malignant cell types observed in the tumor microenvironment.
source: (1) 564 pure ATAC-Seq data of sorted cells were collected to build reference profiles for non-malignant cell types observed in the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

source: (2) Cell-type specific marker peaks were identified using differential accessibility analysis.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

source: (3) Markers with previously observed chromatin accessibility in human healthy tissues were excluded.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

source: (4) For tumor bulk deconvolution, the set of remaining marker peaks was refined by selecting markers with correlated behavior in tumor bulk samples.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

claim: The cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles were integrated into the EPIC-ATAC framework to perform bulk ATAC-Seq deconvolution.
source: (5) The cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles were integrated into the EPIC-ATAC framework to perform bulk ATAC-Seq deconvolution.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

claim: The authors collected 564 samples of sorted cell populations from twelve studies including B cells, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells.
source: To identify robust chromatin accessibility marker peaks of cell types observed in the tumor microenvironment, we collected 564 samples of sorted cell populations from twelve studies including B cells (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022a), CD4+ T cells (Corces et al., 2016; Mumbach et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Giles et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022a), CD8+ T cells (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Giles et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022a), natural killer (NK) cells (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019), dendritic cells (DCs) (mDCs and pDCs are grouped in this cell-type category) (Calderon et al., 2019; Leylek et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020), macrophages (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022a), monocytes (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019; Leylek et al., 2020; Trizzino et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022a), neutrophils (Perez et al., 2020; Ram-Mohan et al., 2021), fibroblasts (Liu et al., 2020; Ge et al., 2021), and endothelial cells (Liu et al., 2020; Xin et al., 2020; Figure 1 box 1, Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented, Figure 1, Figure 2A, and Supplementary file 1. The citations provide additional support.

claim: To limit batch effects, the collected samples were homogeneously processed from read alignment to peak calling.
source: To limit batch effects, the collected samples were homogeneously processed from read alignment to peak calling.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the data processing approach used in the study.

claim: For each cell type, a set of stable peaks observed across samples and studies was derived.
source: For each cell type, we derived a set of stable peaks observed across samples and studies, that is for each study, peaks detected in at least half of the samples were considered, and for each cell type, only peaks detected jointly in all studies were kept (see Materials and methods, 'Generation of an ATAC-Seq reference dataset of non-malignant cell types frequently observed in the tumor microenvironment').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the peak selection approach used in the study.

claim: Pairwise differential analysis was performed to identify marker peaks for each cell type.
source: These peaks were then used to perform pairwise differential analysis to identify marker peaks for each cell type (Figure 1, Box 2).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak identification approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1.

claim: To ensure that the cell-type specific marker peaks are not accessible in other human tissues, ATAC-Seq samples from diverse human tissues from the ENCODE data were included in the differential analysis.
source: To ensure that the cell-type specific marker peaks are not accessible in other human tissues, we included in the differential analysis ATAC-Seq samples from diverse human tissues from the ENCODE data (Abascal et al., 2020; Rozowsky et al., 2023; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak identification approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: The top 200 peaks recurrently differentially accessible across all cell-type pairs were selected as cell-type specific markers.
source: To select a sufficient number of peaks prior to peak filtering, the top 200 peaks recurrently differentially accessible across all cell-type pairs were selected as cell-type specific markers (see Materials and methods, 'Identification of cell-type specific markers').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak selection approach used in the study.

claim: Markers overlapping modules of open chromatin regions accessible in human tissues from the human atlas study were excluded from the marker list.
source: To filter out markers that could be accessible in other human cell types than those included in our reference profiles, we used the human atlas study (Zhang et al., 2021b), which identified modules of open chromatin regions accessible in a comprehensive set of human tissues, and we excluded from our marker list the markers overlapping these modules (Figure 1, box 3, see Materials and methods 'Identification of cell-type specific markers').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak filtering approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1 and a citation.

claim: The resulting marker peaks specific only to the immune cell types were considered for the deconvolution of PBMC samples (PBMC markers).
source: The resulting marker peaks specific only to the immune cell types were considered for the deconvolution of PBMC samples (PBMC markers).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak selection for PBMC deconvolution.

claim: For the deconvolution of tumor bulk samples, the lists of marker peaks specific to fibroblasts and endothelial cells were added to the PBMC markers.
source: For the deconvolution of tumor bulk samples, the lists of marker peaks specific to fibroblasts and endothelial cells were added to the PBMC markers.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak selection for tumor bulk deconvolution.

claim: The extended set of markers for tumor bulk deconvolution was further refined based on the correlation patterns of the markers in tumor bulk samples from diverse solid cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).
source: This extended set of markers was further refined based on the correlation patterns of the markers in tumor bulk samples from the diverse solid cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA; https://www.cancergenomicscloud.org/datasets; Corces et al., 2018), that is markers exhibiting the highest correlation patterns in the tumor bulk samples were selected using the findCorrelation function from the caret R package (Kuhn, 2008; Figure 1, box 4, see the Materials and methods, 'Identification of cell-type specific markers').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak refinement approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1 and citations.

claim: A total of 716 markers of immune, fibroblasts, and endothelial cell types remained after the last filtering (defined as TME markers).
source: A total of 716 markers of immune, fibroblasts, and endothelial cell types remained after the last filtering (defined as TME markers).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data processing and filtering steps described.

claim: The authors recommend using the TME markers and profiles to deconvolve bulk samples from tumor samples and the PBMC markers and profiles to deconvolve PBMC samples.
source: Considering the difference in cell types and the different filtering steps applied on the PBMC and TME markers, we recommend using the TME markers and profiles to deconvolve bulk samples from tumor samples and the PBMC markers and profiles to deconvolve PBMC samples.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the methodological differences between the PBMC and TME marker sets.

claim: Principal component analysis based on each set of marker peaks showed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin.
source: To assess the quality and reproducibility of these markers, we first performed principal component analysis (PCA) based on each set of marker peaks. Computing silhouette coefficients based on the cell-type classification and on the study of origin showed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin (averaged silhouette coefficients above 0.45 for cell type and around 0 for the study of origin).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the PCA analysis and silhouette coefficient calculations.

claim: Averaged silhouette coefficients were above 0.45 for cell type and around 0 for the study of origin.
source: Computing silhouette coefficients based on the cell-type classification and on the study of origin showed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin (averaged silhouette coefficients above 0.45 for cell type and around 0 for the study of origin).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the silhouette coefficient calculations.

claim: The representation of the samples based on the first axes of the PCA confirmed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin.
source: The representation of the samples based on the first axes of the PCA confirmed this observation (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The results indicate limited remaining batch effects after data processing and marker selection.
source: These results indicate limited remaining batch effects after data processing and marker selection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA and silhouette coefficient results.

claim: The collected samples were used to generate chromatin accessibility profiles by computing the average of the normalized counts for each peak in each cell type as well as peak variability in each cell type.
source: We then used the collected samples to generate chromatin accessibility profiles by computing the average of the normalized counts for each peak in each cell type as well as peak variability in each cell type (see Materials and methods) since EPIC uses features variability for the estimation of the cell-type proportions (Racle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the reference profile generation approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: Figure 2C represents the average chromatin accessibility of each marker peak in each cell type of the reference dataset and highlights the cell-type specificity of the selected markers.
source: Figure 2C represents the average chromatin accessibility of each marker peak in each cell type of the reference dataset and highlights, as expected, the cell-type specificity of the selected markers (see also Supplementary files 2 and 3), which was confirmed in independent ATAC-Seq data from sorted cells and single-cell ATAC-Seq samples from blood and diverse human tissues (Figure 2D and E, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2C, Figure 2D, Figure 2E, and Supplementary files 2 and 3.

claim: The cell-type specificity of the selected markers was confirmed in independent ATAC-Seq data from sorted cells and single-cell ATAC-Seq samples from blood and diverse human tissues.
source: Figure 2C represents the average chromatin accessibility of each marker peak in each cell type of the reference dataset and highlights, as expected, the cell-type specificity of the selected markers (see also Supplementary files 2 and 3), which was confirmed in independent ATAC-Seq data from sorted cells and single-cell ATAC-Seq samples from blood and diverse human tissues (Figure 2D and E, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2D and Figure 2E.

claim: Most of the markers are in distal and intergenic regions.
source: We observed that most of the markers are in distal and intergenic regions (Figure 2F), which is expected considering the large proportion of distal regions in the human genome and the fact that such regions have been previously described as highly cell-type specific (Corces et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2F and a citation to prior research.

claim: Distal regions have been previously described as highly cell-type specific.
source: We observed that most of the markers are in distal and intergenic regions (Figure 2F), which is expected considering the large proportion of distal regions in the human genome and the fact that such regions have been previously described as highly cell-type specific (Corces et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Corces et al., 2016).

claim: 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions in contrast to 4% when considering matched genomic regions randomly selected in the set of peaks identified prior to the differential analysis.
source: We also noticed that 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions in contrast to 4% when considering matched genomic regions randomly selected in the set of peaks identified prior to the differential analysis (see Materials and methods), which suggests enrichment in our marker peaks for important regulatory regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the annotation analysis.

claim: The observation that 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions suggests enrichment in marker peaks for important regulatory regions.
source: We also noticed that 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions in contrast to 4% when considering matched genomic regions randomly selected in the set of peaks identified prior to the differential analysis (see Materials and methods), which suggests enrichment in our marker peaks for important regulatory regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of promoter region percentages.

claim: Each marker peak was associated with its nearest gene using ChIP-Enrich based on the 'nearest transcription start site (TSS)' locus definition.
source: To assess the biological relevance of the marker peaks, we associated each marker peak with its nearest gene using ChIP-Enrich based on the 'nearest transcription start site (TSS)' locus definition (Welch et al., 2014; Supplementary files 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak annotation approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, there was an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the JASPAR2022 database.
source: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, we observed an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the JASPAR2022 database (Castro-Mondragon et al., 2022) (using Signac Stuart et al., 2021 and MonaLisa Machlab et al., 2022 for assessing the overrepresentation) and the ReMap catalog (Hammal et al., 2022) (using RemapEnrich, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the enrichment analysis and citations.

claim: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, there was an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the ReMap catalog.
source: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, we observed an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the JASPAR2022 database (Castro-Mondragon et al., 2022) (using Signac Stuart et al., 2021 and MonaLisa Machlab et al., 2022 for assessing the overrepresentation) and the ReMap catalog (Hammal et al., 2022) (using RemapEnrich, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the enrichment analysis and citations.

claim: Based on the 'nearest TSS' annotation, each set of cell-type specific marker peaks was tested for enrichment in regions linked to specific biological pathways (GO pathways) using ChIP-Enrich.
source: Based on the 'nearest TSS' annotation, we tested, using ChIP-Enrich (Welch et al., 2014), whether each set of cell-type specific marker peaks was enriched for regions linked to specific biological pathways (GO pathways).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the pathway enrichment analysis approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: Figure 2G highlights a subset of the enriched pathways that are consistent with prior knowledge of each cell type.
source: Figure 2G highlights a subset of the enriched pathways that are consistent with prior knowledge of each cell type.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2G.

claim: Some of the enriched pathways are known to be characteristic of immune responses to inflammatory or tumoral environments.
source: Some of these pathways are known to be characteristic of immune responses to inflammatory or tumoral environments.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the biological functions of the enriched pathways.

claim: The analyses demonstrate that the proposed cell-type specific marker peaks capture some of the known biological properties associated with each cell type.
source: Overall, these analyses demonstrate that the proposed cell-type specific marker peaks capture some of the known biological properties associated with each cell type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the annotation and enrichment analyses.

claim: The cell-type specific marker peaks and profiles derived from the reference samples were integrated into the EPIC deconvolution tool.
source: The cell-type specific marker peaks and profiles derived from the reference samples were integrated into the EPIC deconvolution tool (Racle et al., 2017; Racle and Gfeller, 2020).
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by citations.

claim: The ATAC-Seq deconvolution framework is referred to as EPIC-ATAC.
source: We will refer to this ATAC-Seq deconvolution framework as EPIC-ATAC.
evidence: This is a naming convention established by the authors.

claim: An option is provided to lift over hg19 datasets to hg38 to ensure the compatibility of any input bulk ATAC-Seq dataset with the EPIC-ATAC marker peaks and reference profiles.
source: To ensure the compatibility of any input bulk ATAC-Seq dataset with the EPIC-ATAC marker peaks and reference profiles, we provide an option to lift over hg19 datasets to hg38 (using the liftOver R package) as the reference profiles are based on the hg38 reference genome.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: The reference profiles are based on the hg38 reference genome.
source: To ensure the compatibility of any input bulk ATAC-Seq dataset with the EPIC-ATAC marker peaks and reference profiles, we provide an option to lift over hg19 datasets to hg38 (using the liftOver R package) as the reference profiles are based on the hg38 reference genome.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: The features of the input bulk matrix are matched to the reference profiles' features.
source: Subsequently, the features of the input bulk matrix are matched to our reference profiles' features.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: To match both sets of features, the distance to the nearest peak in the reference profiles peaks is determined for each peak of the input bulk matrix.
source: To match both sets of features, we determine for each peak of the input bulk matrix the distance to the nearest peak in the reference profiles peaks.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: Overlapping regions are retained and the feature IDs are matched to their associated nearest peaks.
source: Overlapping regions are retained and the feature IDs are matched to their associated nearest peaks.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: If multiple features are matched to the same reference peak, the counts are summed.
source: If multiple features are matched to the same reference peak, the counts are summed.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: Before the estimation of the cell-type proportions, the data are transformed following an approach similar to the transcripts per million (TPM) transformation.
source: Before the estimation of the cell-type proportions, we transform the data following an approach similar to the transcripts per million (TPM) transformation which has been shown to be appropriate for estimating cell fractions from bulk mixtures in RNA-Seq data (Racle et al., 2017; Sturm et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework, supported by citations.

claim: The TPM transformation has been shown to be appropriate for estimating cell fractions from bulk mixtures in RNA-Seq data.
source: Before the estimation of the cell-type proportions, we transform the data following an approach similar to the transcripts per million (TPM) transformation which has been shown to be appropriate for estimating cell fractions from bulk mixtures in RNA-Seq data (Racle et al., 2017; Sturm et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Racle et al., 2017; Sturm et al., 2019).

claim: ATAC-Seq counts are normalized by dividing counts by the peak lengths as well as sample depth and rescaling counts so that the counts of each sample sum to 10^6.
source: We normalize the ATAC-Seq counts by dividing counts by the peak lengths as well as sample depth and rescaling counts so that the counts of each sample sum to 106.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: In RNA-Seq-based deconvolution, EPIC uses an estimation of the amount of mRNA in each reference cell type to derive cell proportions while correcting for cell-type specific mRNA bias.
source: In RNA-Seq-based deconvolution, EPIC uses an estimation of the amount of mRNA in each reference cell type to derive cell proportions while correcting for cell-type specific mRNA bias.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the EPIC framework for RNA-Seq deconvolution.

claim: For the ATAC-Seq-based deconvolution, the values for the amount of mRNA in each reference cell type were set to 1 to give similar weights to all cell-types quantifications.
source: For the ATAC-Seq-based deconvolution, these values were set to 1 to give similar weights to all cell-types quantifications.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claim: ATAC-Seq measures signal at the DNA level, hence the quantity of DNA within each reference cell type is similar.
source: Indeed ATAC-Seq measures signal at the DNA level, hence the quantity of DNA within each reference cell type is similar.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about ATAC-Seq technology.

claim: PBMCs were collected from five healthy donors.
source: To test the accuracy of EPIC-ATAC predictions, we first collected PBMCs from five healthy donors.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the validation experiment.

claim: For each donor, half of the cells were used to generate a bulk ATAC-Seq dataset and the other half was used to determine the cellular composition of each sample by multiparametric flow cytometry.
source: For each donor, half of the cells were used to generate a bulk ATAC-Seq dataset and the other half was used to determine the cellular composition of each sample, that is the proportions of monocytes, B cells, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, NK cells and dendritic cells, by multiparametric flow cytometry (Figure 3A, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the validation experiment, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: EPIC-ATAC was applied to the bulk ATAC-Seq data from five healthy donors.
source: We then applied EPIC-ATAC to the bulk ATAC-Seq data.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the validation experiment.

claim: The predicted cell fractions are consistent with the cell fractions obtained by flow cytometry (Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.78 and root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.10).
source: The predicted cell fractions are consistent with the cell fractions obtained by flow cytometry (Figure 3B, Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.78 and root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.10).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 3B and the statistical measures.

claim: The accuracy of the estimations is variable depending on the samples.
source: However, the accuracy of the estimations is variable depending on the samples.
evidence: This is an observation based on the validation results.

claim: One sample (Sample4) exhibits larger discrepancies between EPIC-ATAC predictions and the ground truth.
source: In particular, one sample (Sample4, star shape in Figure 3B) exhibits larger discrepancies between EPIC-ATAC predictions and the ground truth.
evidence: This is an observation based on the validation results, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Sample4 might be an outlier considering that its cellular composition is similar to that of Samples 2 and 5 but this sample shows particularly high ATAC-Seq accessibility at the monocytes and dendritic marker peaks.
source: Visualizing our marker peaks in the five PBMC samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed that this sample might be an outlier considering that its cellular composition is similar to that of Samples 2 and 5 but this sample shows particularly high ATAC-Seq accessibility at the monocytes and dendritic marker peaks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the visualization of marker peaks in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The high ATAC-Seq accessibility at the monocytes and dendritic marker peaks in Sample4 could explain why EPIC-ATAC overestimates the proportions of the two populations in this case.
source: This could explain why EPIC-ATAC overestimates the proportions of the two populations in this case.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of high ATAC-Seq accessibility at specific marker peaks.

claim: EPIC-ATAC was applied to pseudobulk PBMC samples generated using three publicly available PBMC scATAC-Seq datasets.
source: As a second validation, we applied EPIC-ATAC to pseudobulk PBMC samples (referred to as the PBMC pseudobulk dataset), generated using three publicly available PBMC scATAC-Seq datasets (Granja et al., 2019; Satpathy et al., 2019; 10x Genomics, 2021; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the validation experiment, supported by citations.

claim: A high correlation (0.91) between EPIC-ATAC predictions and true cell-type proportions and a low RMSE (0.05) were observed for the PBMC pseudobulk dataset.
source: A high correlation (0.91) between EPIC-ATAC predictions and true cell-type proportions and a low RMSE (0.05) were observed for this dataset (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 3C and the statistical measures.

claim: The accuracy of the predictions obtained with EPIC-ATAC was compared with the accuracy of other deconvolution approaches which could be used with the reference profiles and marker peaks.
source: The accuracy of the predictions obtained with EPIC-ATAC was then compared with the accuracy of other deconvolution approaches which could be used with our reference profiles and marker peaks (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the benchmarking analysis, supported by Figure 3D–E.

claim: The benchmarking considered DeconPeaker, CIBERSORTx, quanTIseq, ABIS, and MCPcounter.
source: To this end, we considered both the DeconPeaker method (Li et al., 2020b) originally developed for bulk ATAC-Seq as well as several algorithms developed for bulk RNA-Seq (CIBERSORTx Newman et al., 2019), quanTIseq (Finotello et al., 2019), ABIS (Monaco et al., 2019), and MCPcounter (Becht et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the benchmarking analysis, supported by citations.

claim: The marker peaks and profiles derived in this work were used in each of the benchmarking methods.
source: To enable meaningful comparison across the cell types considered in this work and use the method initially developed for bulk RNA-Seq deconvolution, the marker peaks and profiles derived in this work were used in each of these methods (See Materials and methods, 'Benchmarking of the EPIC-ATAC framework against other existing deconvolution tools').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the benchmarking analysis.

claim: DeconPeaker and CIBERSORTx include the option to define cell-type specific markers and profiles from a set of reference samples.
source: DeconPeaker and CIBERSORTx also include the option to define cell-type specific markers and profiles from a set of reference samples.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the capabilities of DeconPeaker and CIBERSORTx.

claim: The ATAC-Seq samples collection was fed to DeconPeaker and CIBERSORTx and the resulting profiles and marker peaks were used to perform bulk ATAC-Seq deconvolution.
source: We thus additionally fed our ATAC-Seq samples collection to both algorithms and used the resulting profiles and marker peaks to perform bulk ATAC-Seq deconvolution.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the benchmarking analysis.

claim: The resulting predictions from DeconPeaker and CIBERSORTx using custom profiles are referred to as DeconPeaker-Custom and CIBERSORTx-Custom.
source: The resulting predictions are referred to as DeconPeaker-Custom and CIBERSORTx-Custom.
evidence: This is a naming convention established by the authors.

claim: Many tools displayed high correlation and low RMSE values, similar to those of EPIC-ATAC, and no single tool consistently outperformed the others.
source: Many tools displayed high correlation and low RMSE values, similar to those of EPIC-ATAC, and no single tool consistently outperformed the others (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the benchmarking analysis, supported by Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fact that the marker peaks and reference profiles could be used with EPIC-ATAC and other existing tools demonstrates their broad applicability.
source: The fact that our marker peaks and reference profiles could be used with EPIC-ATAC and other existing tools demonstrates their broad applicability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the benchmarking results.

claim: The ability of the EPIC-ATAC framework to predict not only immune and stromal cell proportions but also the proportion of cells for which reference profiles are not available (i.e. uncharacterized cells) was evaluated.
source: We evaluated the ability of the EPIC-ATAC framework to predict not only immune and stromal cell proportions but also the proportion of cells for which reference profiles are not available (i.e. uncharacterized cells).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the validation experiment.

claim: Two previously published scATAC-Seq datasets containing basal cell carcinoma and gynecological cancer samples were considered for evaluation.
source: For this purpose, we considered two previously published scATAC-Seq datasets containing basal cell carcinoma and gynecological cancer samples (Satpathy et al., 2019; Regner et al., 2021) as well as the samples from the Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN; https://data.humantumoratlas.org/) single-cell multiome dataset composed of samples from diverse cancer types (Terekhanova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the validation experiment, supported by citations.

claim: Pseudobulks were generated by averaging the chromatin accessibility signal across all cells of each sample for each dataset.
source: For each dataset, we generated pseudobulks by averaging the chromatin accessibility signal across all cells of each sample (see Materials and methods, 'Datasets used for the evaluation of ATAC-Seq deconvolution').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the validation experiment.

claim: Applying EPIC-ATAC to each dataset shows that this framework can simultaneously predict the proportions of both uncharacterized cells and immune, stromal and vascular cells.
source: Applying EPIC-ATAC to each dataset shows that this framework can simultaneously predict the proportions of both uncharacterized cells and immune, stromal and vascular cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: In basal cell carcinoma and gynecological cancer samples, the proportion of uncharacterized cells can be seen as a proxy for the proportion of cancer cells.
source: In basal cell carcinoma and gynecological cancer samples, the proportion of uncharacterized cells can be seen as a proxy for the proportion of cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the composition of the samples.

claim: In the HTAN dataset, some of the samples also contain cell types that are neither immune, fibroblasts or endothelial cells nor malignant cells.
source: In the HTAN dataset, some of the samples also contain cell types that are neither immune, fibroblasts or endothelial cells nor malignant cells.
evidence: This is an observation based on the composition of the HTAN dataset.

claim: The uncharacterized cells in the HTAN samples group cancer and normal cells from the tumor site.
source: Hence, the uncharacterized cells in these samples group cancer and normal cells from the tumor site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the composition of the HTAN samples.

claim: EPIC-ATAC was able to not only estimate the proportion of cell types included in the TME reference profiles but also the proportion of uncharacterized cells in most of the cancer types.
source: EPIC-ATAC, in this context, was able to not only estimate the proportion of cell types included in the TME reference profiles but also the proportion of uncharacterized cells in most of the cancer types (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The performances of EPIC-ATAC were compared to other existing deconvolution tools on the cancer datasets.
source: As for the PBMC datasets, we compared EPIC-ATAC performances to other existing deconvolution tools (see Materials and methods, 'Benchmarking of the EPIC-ATAC framework against other existing deconvolution tools').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the benchmarking analysis.

claim: For each dataset, EPIC-ATAC led to the highest performances and was the only method to accurately predict the proportion of uncharacterized cells.
source: For each dataset, EPIC-ATAC led to the highest performances and was the only method to accurately predict the proportion of uncharacterized cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the benchmarking analysis, supported by Figure 4B and related figure supplements.

claim: Although quanTIseq also allows users to perform predictions of uncharacterized cells, the method resulted in lower correlation and higher RMSE values when comparing the estimated and true proportions of the uncharacterized cells.
source: Although quanTIseq also allows users to perform such predictions, the method resulted in lower correlation and higher RMSE values when comparing the estimated and true proportions of the uncharacterized cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the benchmarking analysis, supported by Figure 4B and related figure supplements.

claim: In the EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq frameworks, predictions correspond to absolute cell-type fractions which include the proportion of uncharacterized cells.
source: In the EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq frameworks, predictions correspond to absolute cell-type fractions which include the proportion of uncharacterized cells, that is proportions of all cells present in the bulk, while the estimations obtained from the other tools correspond to relative cell fractions, that is proportions of cells present in the reference profiles (CIBERSORTx, DeconPeaker) or to scores with arbitrary units (ABIS, MCPcounter) without considering the presence of uncharacterized cells.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the different types of outputs from different deconvolution tools.

claim: The estimations obtained from CIBERSORTx and DeconPeaker correspond to relative cell fractions.
source: In the EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq frameworks, predictions correspond to absolute cell-type fractions which include the proportion of uncharacterized cells, that is proportions of all cells present in the bulk, while the estimations obtained from the other tools correspond to relative cell fractions, that is proportions of cells present in the reference profiles (CIBERSORTx, DeconPeaker) or to scores with arbitrary units (ABIS, MCPcounter) without considering the presence of uncharacterized cells.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the different types of outputs from different deconvolution tools.

claim: The estimations obtained from ABIS and MCPcounter correspond to scores with arbitrary units without considering the presence of uncharacterized cells.
source: In the EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq frameworks, predictions correspond to absolute cell-type fractions which include the proportion of uncharacterized cells, that is proportions of all cells present in the bulk, while the estimations obtained from the other tools correspond to relative cell fractions, that is proportions of cells present in the reference profiles (CIBERSORTx, DeconPeaker) or to scores with arbitrary units (ABIS, MCPcounter) without considering the presence of uncharacterized cells.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the different types of outputs from different deconvolution tools.

claim: For the tools that do not predict uncharacterized cells, the uncharacterized cells estimations were fixed to 0.
source: For the latter group of tools, we fixed the uncharacterized cells estimations to 0.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the benchmarking analysis.

claim: This approach provides a clear and significant advantage to EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq.
source: This approach provides a clear and significant advantage to EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the benchmarking results, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: A second benchmark was conducted excluding the predictions of uncharacterized cell fractions and rescaling both estimations and true proportions to sum to 1.
source: For this reason, wconducted a second benchmark excluding the predictions of uncharacterized cell fractions and rescaling both estimations and true proportions to sum to 1 (see Materials and methods, 'Benchmarking of the EPIC-ATAC framework against other existing deconvolution tools').
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the benchmarking analysis.

claim: EPIC-ATAC outperformed most of the other methods also when excluding the uncharacterized cells.
source: EPIC-ATAC outperformed most of the other methods also when excluding the uncharacterized cells (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the benchmarking analysis, supported by Figure 4C and related figure supplements.

claim: All the tools require a limited amount of time and memory to run, that is less than 20 s in average.
source: Note that in terms of computational resources, all the tools require a limited amount of time and memory to run, that is less than 20 s in average (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the benchmarking analysis, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: EPIC-ATAC predictions were evaluated in each major cell type separately in the different benchmarking datasets to investigate the impact of cell type abundance on the accuracy of ATAC-Seq deconvolution.
source: To investigate the impact of cell type abundance on the accuracy of ATAC-Seq deconvolution, we evaluated EPIC-ATAC predictions in each major cell type separately in the different benchmarking datasets (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: NK cells, endothelial cells, neutrophils, or dendritic cells showed lower correlation values.
source: NK cells, endothelial cells, neutrophils, or dendritic cells showed lower correlation values.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the analysis, supported by the data.

claim: The lower correlation values for NK cells, endothelial cells, neutrophils, or dendritic cells can be explained by the fact that these cell types are low-abundant in the benchmarking datasets.
source: These values can be explained by the fact that these cell types are low-abundant in our benchmarking datasets (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of lower correlation values and the abundance of these cell types, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: For the endothelial cells and dendritic cells, the RMSE values associated with these cell types remain low.
source: For the endothelial cells and dendritic cells, the RMSE values associated with these cell types remain low.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the analysis, supported by the data.

claim: While the predictions of EPIC-ATAC might not be precise enough to compare endothelial cells and dendritic cells proportions between different samples, the cell-type quantification within each sample is reliable.
source: This suggests that while the predictions of EPIC-ATAC might not be precise enough to compare these cell-type proportions between different samples, the cell-type quantification within each sample is reliable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of low RMSE values despite lower correlation values.

claim: For the NK cells and the neutrophils, more variability with higher RMSE values in some datasets was observed which suggests that the markers and profiles for these cell types might be improved.
source: For the NK cells and the neutrophils, we observed more variability with higher RMSE values in some datasets which suggests that the markers and profiles for these cell types might be improved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of higher RMSE values for these cell types.

claim: The predictions from the other deconvolution tools are more reliable for the frequent cell types.
source: As for EPIC-ATAC, the predictions from the other deconvolution tools are more reliable for the frequent cell types.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the benchmarking analysis, supported by the data in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The authors evaluated whether EPIC-ATAC could predict the proportions of T-cell subtypes to explore the accuracy of ATAC-Seq deconvolution for more related cell types.
source: To explore the accuracy of ATAC-Seq deconvolution for more related cell types, we evaluated whether EPIC-ATAC could predict the proportions of T-cell subtypes.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis.

claim: Naive and non-naive CD8+ as well as naive, helper/memory and regulatory CD4+ T cells (Tregs) were considered.
source: To this end, we considered naive and non-naive CD8+ as well as naive, helper/memory and regulatory CD4+ T cells (Tregs).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis.

claim: The list of cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles was redefined including the five T-cell subtypes.
source: We redefined our list of cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles including also these five T-cell subtypes (Supplementary files 8-9, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A) and observed that the markers were conserved in external data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis, supported by Supplementary files 8-9 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The markers for T-cell subtypes were conserved in external data.
source: We redefined our list of cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles including also these five T-cell subtypes (Supplementary files 8-9, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A) and observed that the markers were conserved in external data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the analysis, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The more detailed cell-type annotation of the PBMC datasets as well as the basal cell carcinoma dataset was used to evaluate the EPIC-ATAC predictions of cell-subtype fractions using the updated markers and profiles.
source: We capitalized on the more detailed cell-type annotation of the PBMC datasets as well as the basal cell carcinoma dataset to evaluate the EPIC-ATAC predictions of cell-subtype fractions using these updated markers and profiles.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the analysis.

claim: Overall, the correlations observed between the predictions and true proportions of T cells decreased when considering T-cell subtypes rather than CD4+ and CD8+ cell types only.
source: Overall, the correlations observed between the predictions and true proportions of T cells decreased when considering T-cell subtypes rather than CD4+ and CD8+ cell types only (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the analysis, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Low accuracies were obtained for helper/memory CD4+ and naive T-cell subtypes.
source: In particular, low accuracies were obtained for helper/memory CD4+ and naive T-cell subtypes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the analysis, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Similar results were obtained using other deconvolution tools when considering T-cell subtypes.
source: Similar results were obtained using other deconvolution tools (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the analysis, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: EPIC-ATAC was applied to a breast cancer cohort of 42 breast ATAC-Seq samples including samples from two breast cancer subtypes.
source: We applied EPIC-ATAC to a breast cancer cohort of 42 breast ATAC-Seq samples including samples from two breast cancer subtypes, that is 35 oestrogen receptor (ER)-positive human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative (ER+/HER2-) breast cancer samples and 7 triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) samples (Kumegawa et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the application of EPIC-ATAC, supported by a citation.

claim: No cell sorting was performed in parallel to the chromatin accessibility sequencing in the breast cancer cohort.
source: No cell sorting was performed in parallel to the chromatin accessibility sequencing.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the breast cancer cohort.

claim: The authors of the breast cancer cohort study used a set of cell-type specific cis-regulatory elements (CREs) identified in scATAC-Seq data from similar breast cancer samples and estimated the amount of infiltration of each cell type by averaging the ATAC-Seq signal of each set of cell-type specific CREs in their samples.
source: For this reason, the authors used a set of cell-type specific cis-regulatory elements (CREs) identified in scATAC-Seq data from similar breast cancer samples (Kumegawa et al., 2022) and estimated the amount of infiltration of each cell type by averaging the ATAC-Seq signal of each set of cell-type specific CREs in their samples.
evidence: This statement is based on the methods used in the original breast cancer cohort study, supported by a citation.

claim: EPIC-ATAC was used to estimate the proportions of different cell types of the TME in the breast cancer cohort.
source: We used EPIC-ATAC to estimate the proportions of different cell types of the TME.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the application of EPIC-ATAC.
